title: A Complete Classroom Management Guide for an Enjoyable and Productive Learning Environment
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Built around the recommendations of classroom-management coach Lynsay Mills Fabio and Michael Linsin of Smart Classroom Management, this guide gives Stuart's complete system: a short, clear list of five rules and a three-step consequence sequence, teacher moves that prevent misbehavior, teacher moves that respond to misbehavior, and routines for recurring whole-class moments. He closes with a CARE framework, Constancy, Awe, Relationships, Excellence, for keeping a well-managed room from feeling cold or robotic.
points: Stuart's five classroom rules deliberately avoid vague catch-alls like respect yourself and others, reasoning that clarity, like a specific speed limit versus drive safely, reduces disputes and makes enforcement consistent.
His three-step consequence sequence is designed to be delivered with emotional neutrality, likened explicitly to a traffic officer issuing a ticket rather than a personal confrontation.
He rejects student-generated classroom rules as impractical at scale, citing years of experimentation that produced widely varying results across multiple class sections for too much time investment.
The CARE framework exists to keep a rules-and-consequences system from curdling into a soulless exercise in human robotics, treating warmth as a structural requirement, not an accident.
quotes: Classroom management — that is, creating an environment in which student behaviors are conducive to enjoyable and productive learning — is the first hurdle a teacher must cross.

Imagine if the speed limit in my neighborhood was drive at a safe speed rather than 25 mph. Driving speed would vary greatly in such a scenario, officers would have a much harder time giving tickets, and tickets would be much easier to challenge in court.

In other words: do everything you can to make rules and consequences a clinical, matter-of-fact concept. There is no reason to ever shame a student with these things — everyone has off days, some more than others.
I have experimented in the past with student-created classroom rules. The trouble I've had with this is that it takes a lot of time and the results vary widely.
No matter how good I am at teaching, misbehavior still happens. All that I need to approach this misbehavior with grace and emotional neutrality is to imagine what it's like being a student.
This CARE Framework for warmth — Constancy, Awe, Relationships, Excellence — provides both the foundation and the capstone for a well-managed classroom.
